{{otherpeople|Richard Davison}}
 
'''Richard Joseph "Dick" Davisson''' (December 29, 1922 &ndash; June 15, 2004) was an American [[physicist]].

Davisson was the son of [[Clinton Davisson]], a Nobel laureate, and his wife Charlotte; Davisson's maternal uncle, Sir [[Owen Richardson]], was also a Nobel laureate.<ref name=ST>[https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20040624/davissonobit24m/dick-davisson-retired-uw-physicist-dies-at-81    The Seattle Times website, ''Dick Davisson, retired UW physicist, dies at 81'', article by Keith Ervin and Diane Brooks dated June 24, 2004]</ref>

During [[World War II]] he worked on the [[Manhattan Project]] as part of the [[Special Engineer Detachment]].<ref>[https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/voices/oral-histories/benjamin-bedersons-interview/    Nuclear Museum website, Voices of the Manhattan Project section,  ''Benjamin Bederson’s Interview'']</ref>  At [[Los Alamos National Laboratory|Los Alamos]], he met Professor [[Robert Williams (scientist)|Robert Williams]], who later recruited him to teach at the [[University of Washington]].

As a graduate student at Cornell after World War II, Davisson built a [[cosmic ray]] machine that would do everything but write a grad student's thesis.{{citation needed|date=July 2011}} He acquired a huge magnet from Navy surplus, built a [[cloud chamber]] and a set of Geiger counters and designed a universal-focus camera to record cosmic ray events. Then he designed and built an early electronic computer to record and sort the events according to energy, mass, charge, direction and frequency. Davisson went on to the University of Washington without a PhD.

Davisson was a member of the University of Washington's team which designed a system for detecting [[subatomic particle]]s known as [[muon]]s.<ref name=ST /> After the U.S. government pulled the funding on the [[Superconducting Super Collider]] project, the team was recruited by [[CERN]] to help build part of the muon [[particle detector|detector]] of the [[A Toroidal LHC ApparatuS|ATLAS]] experiment in the [[Large Hadron Collider]] [[particle accelerator]], in which Davisson took part, e.g., creating tools to test the detector tubes and as a liaison between the University of Washington's team and the rest of the collaborating group.

Davisson retired in 2000, at the age of 77.<ref name=ST /> He was married for forty years to Elizabeth "Betty" Davisson, a retired psychiatric social worker from whom he separated after fourteen years. They had one son.<ref>[https://bonneywatson.com/obituary/richard-dick-davisson/    Bonney Watson website, ''Richard ‘Dick’ Davisson'']</ref>
